fields.h1: How to Trust God in Suffering When Life Hurts
fields.meta_title: How to Trust God in Suffering When Life Hurts
fields.description: When suffering comes, “trust God” can feel impossible. Here is what the Christians who suffered most learned about holding on to God — and how to begin.
fields.body_html:
When you are in real pain — a diagnosis you didn’t expect, a grave you didn’t think you’d be standing at yet, a marriage coming apart in your hands, a prayer that has gone unanswered for years — the instruction to “just trust God” can feel almost cruel. Trust him to do what? He has not stopped the thing that is breaking you.

So it helps to know that the people who wrote the enduring Christian books on suffering were not writing from a comfortable distance. They wrote from inside it. And what they found, again and again, is that trusting God in suffering is not a feeling you manufacture or a brave face you paste over the wound. It is something quieter and far sturdier: a decision to keep holding on to a God you have good reason to believe is already holding on to you. Here is what they learned.

Trusting God is not pretending it doesn't hurt

The first thing to say is the thing most often missed: the Bible never asks you to deny your pain. It is full of people who trusted God and wept, argued, and asked “how long?” A third of the Psalms are laments. When Lazarus died, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35) — the shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the most comforting, because it means God in the flesh did not stand aloof from grief. Job, scraping his sores in the ashes, could say both “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” and, in the same breath, argue his anguish to God’s face (Job 13:15).

Trust and honesty are not opposites. Honesty is where real trust begins, because a God you cannot be honest with is not a God you actually trust — he is one you are managing. And it is to exactly such sufferers that the promise comes: “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18). Not near to those who pretend. Near to the broken.

God is working even the worst of it toward good

Thomas Watson, a Puritan pastor ejected from his pulpit who knew hard years, wrote an entire book on a single verse: “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). His title says it plainly — All Things for Good.

Watson is careful about what this does and does not mean. It does not mean the suffering is itself good, or that you must call evil a blessing. It means God is a workman skilled enough to take even the thing that is harming you and bend it toward a good you cannot yet see. He uses the old image of the goldsmith: the fire is not the enemy of the gold; it is how the impurities come loose and the gold comes clean. The pain is real. But it is not the last word, and it is not without purpose in the hands of the One who permits it.

The comfort you need is a Person, not an explanation

When we suffer, what we usually want is an answer to “why?” What God more often gives is himself. Hannah Whitall Smith, who buried four of her seven children, wrote a book whose title is its whole argument: The God of All Comfort. She had learned it from Paul, who blesses “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

Explanations, even true ones, do not hold a breaking heart; a Person does. Smith’s counsel is not to wait until you understand before you trust, but to let God be enough before you understand anything at all. Comfort, she insists, is not the removal of the trouble but the nearness of God inside it — and that nearness is available now, in the dark, before a single question is answered.

What matters is not how heavy the pressure is, but where it rests

Hudson Taylor spent fifty years as a missionary in China and buried a wife and several children there. He knew crushing pressure — and he left one of the most quietly freeing things ever said about it:

It doesn’t matter, really, how great the pressure is. It only matters where the pressure lies. See that it never comes between you and the Lord — then, the greater the pressure, the more it presses you to His breast.Hudson Taylor

This is not a trick for feeling less. It is a reorientation. Suffering will press on you; the question is which direction it drives you. God had promised as much through Isaiah: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned” (Isaiah 43:2). Not if the waters come, but when — and the promise is not exemption from the fire but his presence in it.

Learning to kiss the wave

Charles Spurgeon, the most famous preacher of his century, lived with lifelong depression and painful illness. Faith never made suffering theoretical for him. And he said something that has steadied countless sufferers since:

I have learned to kiss the wave that throws me against the Rock of Ages.Charles Spurgeon

He does not say the wave is gentle, or that he has stopped feeling it. He says the very wave that knocks him down also throws him onto the one unmovable thing — Christ, the Rock. In his sermon Consolation in the Furnace, Spurgeon reminds sufferers that God is not absent from the fire but present in it, as he was with the three men in Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace. And he leaned, as we all must, on the grace God gave Paul in his own unrelieved suffering: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

But what if it doesn't get better?

Much of what passes for comfort quietly assumes the trouble will lift — hold on, and the storm will pass. But some storms do not pass. The illness is chronic. The person does not come back. The prayer, after years, is still unanswered. What then?

Here the Bible is more honest than most of our encouragement. Paul begged God three times to remove his “thorn in the flesh,” and God said no — not because he did not love Paul, but because he had something better than removal to give him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The thorn stayed. The grace came. Job, for his part, never received the explanation he demanded; God answered him not with reasons but with himself, and it was enough. And countless psalms end not with the problem solved but with the sufferer choosing, in the dark, to hope in God anyway.

This is the deepest form of trust, and the costliest: to keep holding on when the thing you asked for is not given, believing that the God who withholds the lesser gift is giving a greater one you cannot yet see. It does not mean pretending the loss is fine. It means saying, with Job, “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15) — that even if it never gets better on this side of eternity, God is still good, still near, and still worth trusting. That kind of trust is not natural. It is forged, slowly, in exactly the fire that seems to be destroying it.

How to actually trust God today

None of this happens all at once. But the same writers who suffered leave a few practical, repeatable steps for the day you are actually in:

  • Tell God the truth. Pray the lament, not the performance. “How long?” is a prayer. He can bear your honesty far better than your pretending.
  • Stay near his word, especially when it feels dry. You are keeping company with him until the ground under your feet steadies. A single verse is enough for a hard day.
  • Don’t carry it alone. Suffering isolates; that is part of how it works. Let the body of Christ pray for you and sit with you.
  • Take it one day at a time. His mercies “are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23) — today’s supply for today’s trouble. Do not try to trust him for the whole future at once.
  • Look back. Remember the times he has already carried you through what you were sure would end you. A trust that remembers is far harder to shake.

Trusting God in suffering, in the end, is not the absence of pain and not the manufacture of strength. It is the decision — made again each morning, sometimes each hour — to keep holding the hand that is holding you. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1). You do not have to feel strong. You only have to not let go — and even your grip, on the hardest days, is held by a stronger one than yours.
